paras: The Lincolnton riot arrests and banishment took place in Lincolnton, North Carolina, in December 1882, when thirty Black men were jailed for a riot and, after trial, all but one were acquitted on condition that they leave the town. Wire reports of armed patrols, threats to burn the town and troops ordered to the scene spread nationally before dispatches from Charlotte and Lincolnton denied that any renewed trouble had occurred.

According to a Raleigh dispatch of December 21, the trouble originated in an attack of train hands on the paymaster, with about 100 people engaged in the disturbances. The papers name neither the paymaster nor the railroad, and they do not state the train hands' race or the cause of the attack.

The Town Commissioners met and called out the local military company, which arrested thirty of what the dispatch called 'the leading rioters'. The prisoners were held in the jail, which troops guarded for three nights, while citizens kept up patrols and a constant watch over the town. A Lincolnton dispatch of December 19 said that 'negro incendiaries' had made several attempts to burn the town, whereas the Raleigh account spoke only of repeated threats to do so.

On the afternoon of December 21 the Governor received a telegram that the trouble had begun afresh, and the Adjutant General ordered troops to Lincolnton. Two days later Raleigh reported that nothing further had been heard, that Captain Hakes's company had been ordered to act with the sheriff as a posse, and that the expected outbreak was thought not to have happened.

A dispatch from Lincolnton dated December 28 reported that the thirty men had been tried and all but one acquitted, on condition that they leave the place. The remaining defendant was, in the Wheeling Register's words, 'charged with an attempt to kill the town marshal', while Baltimore's Der Deutsche Correspondent said he was found guilty of attempting to murder Marshal Towers. None of the defendants is named, and no report of a sentence was found.

The story reached readers almost entirely through two wire dispatches, the Lincolnton report of December 19 and the Raleigh report of December 21, carried from Savannah and Washington to Augusta, Maine, and in German translation in Baltimore and Chicago. Headlines cast the episode as a racial disorder: the Union Times of South Carolina called it 'A Negro Rior [Riot]', and the Daily Kennebec Journal headed it 'A Lawless Community' and 'Under Martial Law', adding that 'a bad riot' was feared. The New-York Tribune reduced it to one line in its news summary, saying 'the negroes threatened to burn the village'.

Within days the alarm was contradicted: a Charlotte dispatch relayed from Richmond said there was 'no foundation' for the riot report, and the Wilmington Star's Lincolnton correspondent wrote that there had been no trouble for eight or ten days and no request for troops. The acquittals and the condition of leaving town drew only brief notices, in the Wheeling Register and the German-language Correspondent. No Black-press coverage survives in the collection for this year, and no account from the arrested men or the train hands appears.

Whether trouble resumed on December 21 is disputed: Raleigh reports said it had begun afresh, while the Lincolnton correspondent of the Wilmington Star, the most local source, denied any trouble for more than a week. The reports also differ on whether Black residents actually tried to burn the town or only threatened to, and on whether the thirtieth defendant was convicted or only charged.

reader.title: Lincolnton riot arrests and banishment (1882)
bases: The papers describe a riot begun by an attack of train hands on a paymaster, the arrest and jailing of thirty Black men by the town's military company, armed citizen patrols, and a court outcome that freed 29 of them only on condition that they leave the town (A8, A30, A31); no white mob attack on Black residents is reported, so no single anti-Black violence category fits.

Separate dispatches from Lincolnton (A1, A2), Raleigh (A8, A11) and a later Lincolnton report of the trials (A30, A31) agree on the riot and the thirty arrests, and the Wilmington Star's Lincolnton correspondent places trouble eight or ten days before Dec. 25 (A25); only the reported renewed outbreak of Dec. 21 is contested (A20, A25).

accounts.label: Lincolnton wire, Dec. 19
accounts.gist: Thirty Black men jailed for a riot several days earlier; trials to begin; citizens' patrols guard the town and 'negro incendiaries' have tried several times to burn it.

accounts.label: Raleigh wire, Dec. 21
accounts.gist: The riot began with an attack of train hands on the paymaster; the military company arrested thirty of about 100; Black residents threatened to burn the town; the Governor heard that trouble had begun afresh and troops were ordered.

accounts.label: Charlotte and Lincolnton denials
accounts.gist: A Charlotte dispatch via Richmond and a Lincolnton special to the Wilmington Star said the report of a renewed riot had no foundation, there had been no trouble for eight or ten days, and no troops had been requested.

accounts.label: Lincolnton wire, Dec. 28
accounts.gist: All but one of the thirty were acquitted on condition of leaving the town; one was held for an attempt on the town marshal's life.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Dec. 19 and Dec. 21 wires unaltered, describing 'negro incendiaries' and threats 'by the negroes to burn the town'.

The Daily Kennebec Journal headlined the story 'A Lawless Community' and 'Under Martial Law' and added that 'a bad riot' was feared, while later dispatches from Charlotte and the Wilmington Star denied any renewed trouble.

record_check.dossier: Riot after an attack on a railroad paymaster, mass arrest by the town's military company, and banishment of 29 acquitted Black men as the condition of acquittal; best coded 'other' (or expulsion, if the banishment is the focus).
The arrests were made by the local military company called out by the Town Commissioners; citizens patrolled; a posse is mentioned only for Dec. 23.
Thirty Black men were jailed under guard and tried.
Thirty unnamed Black men arrested; 29 acquitted on condition of leaving town.

record_check.dossier: Add the paymaster origin, the contested renewed outbreak of Dec. 21, and the Dec. 28 acquittals conditioned on leaving town.

info: A riot 'several days' before Dec. 19, 1882; a Lincolnton correspondent on about Dec. 23-25 said there had been no trouble for eight or ten days.
The thirty Black men were jailed for being 'concerned in the riot'; the riot was said to have originated in an attack of train hands on the paymaster.
One defendant was found guilty (A30) or remained charged (A31) with an attempt to kill the town marshal, named Towers in A30.
